the process/composition columns (NT, THT, THt, THQCr, CT, Ct, DT, Dt, QmT,
TT, Tt, TCr, C, Si, Mn, P, S, Ni, Cr, Cu, Mo, RedRatio, dA, dB, dC) and
column `target` (the measured rotating-bending fatigue strength (MPa)).

turns.answer_text:
## Analysis

Scanning the target column, I see three distinct "regimes" in the data:

1. **Low-temper regime** (NT≈825–885, THT=30, CT/DT/TT≈30): targets 225–400 MPa.
2. **Mid quench-temper regime** (NT≈845–900, THT≈845–865, THQCr=8–24, CT=30, TT≈490–680, TCr≈24): targets climb steadily from ~360 up to ~600–718 MPa as TT increases and alloying (Cr, Ni) rises. The highest members of this group (target 688, 718) have C≈0.53–0.62, Si≈0.3–1.5, Cr≈0.67–0.75, RedRatio≈600–800, TT≈490–500, TCr=24.
3. **High-CT/DT regime** (NT=930, THT=30, CT=930, Ct/DT/Dt large, TT=160–200, Tt=120, TCr=0.5): targets jump to 900–1190 MPa.

There is no directly observed sample near 800 MPa — the data has a gap between the top of regime 2 (~700–720) and the bottom of regime 3 (~900). To hit 800 MPa, I interpolate linearly between the closest lower sample (target=718, from regime 2) and the closest higher sample (target=900, from regime 3), using weight t=(800-718)/(900-718)=0.45, blending all 25 variables proportionally. This keeps every variable within its observed/allowed range while landing near the desired 800 MPa target.
